analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers refinance federal student loans at the 10-year Treasury rate plus one percent.
analysis.headline: Despite 28 cosponsors including two Republicans, the bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee in October 2017 and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let people with older federal student loans refinance them at a new fixed rate equal to the 10-year Treasury rate plus one percentage point — well below the rates most existing loans carry. It would also lower rates on all new federal loans going forward, cap them, repeal the origination fee charged on federal loans, let medical and dental residents put off payments during training, and make sure refinancing doesn't erase progress borrowers have made toward loan forgiveness plans. It died in the House committee it was assigned to.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 million Americans holding federal student loans, especially those stuck with older loans or FFEL loans carrying interest rates above 6-7%. Refinancing at Treasury plus 1% would cut monthly interest costs; repealing origination fees saves every new borrower roughly 1% of their loan up front; medical and dental residents gain payment relief during low-paid training years.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers repaying high-interest federal student loans

how_it_helps.text: The Education Department would reissue Direct Loans and older FFEL loans at a fixed rate equal to the 10-year Treasury yield plus 1%, covering unpaid principal, accrued interest, and late charges.

Rates on all new loans would also be set at Treasury plus 1%, capped at 8.25% for undergraduates, 9.5% for graduate students, and 10.5% for PLUS loans — a formula tied to what the government itself borrows for, rather than a markup.
The origination fee charged on federal Direct Loans would be repealed, so future borrowers would no longer lose roughly 1% of their loan before receiving a dollar of it.
Borrowers in medical or dental internship or residency programs could defer payments until their programs end, and low-income borrowers would pay no interest during deferral.
Refinancing would not erase progress toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness or income-based repayment: payments made on the original loan would count toward the required payment totals.
Eligibility rules would be set to prioritize borrowers with the greatest financial need, and the bill forbids stretching out the repayment term, limiting the cost to the government.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government — meaning taxpayers generally — would collect far less interest revenue from the loan program, and FFEL-program banks would have their loans paid off early. In the current system, federal loans charge rates well above what the Treasury pays to borrow, and that spread has been used to fund other education programs and deficit reduction.

drawbacks.text: The bill costs money. Refinancing loans at Treasury plus 1% and repealing origination fees eliminates the interest spread and fees the federal loan program currently generates, revenue that in recent years has helped fund Pell Grants and offset deficits.

Borrowers who refinance an FFEL loan would start fresh on Public Service Loan Forgiveness: only payments made after the refinancing would count, a trap for public-sector workers who switch loans midway.
Help is not automatic: the bill lets the Education Department set income and debt-to-income eligibility rules, so some borrowers could be excluded at the Department's discretion.
It only covers loans disbursed before July 1, 2017 for refinancing, so its relief is one-time rather than a permanent safety valve for future cohorts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The borrower relief is real and targeted: lower rates on loans already on the books, cheaper new loans, no origination fees, and protection for forgiveness programs. The honest cost is that the government would earn less on its loan portfolio — a cost that falls on taxpayers broadly rather than on any single industry, and the bill's design choices (no term extension, need-based eligibility, temporary refinancing window) keep the total score manageable. The FFEL forgiveness-credit reset is a genuine design flaw for a narrow group of public-sector borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee — controlled by the Republican majority — never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Garamendi introduced the bill on October 10, 2017, with an initial group of 15 cosponsors joining at introduction.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
It gathered 28 cosponsors in total, 26 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
That was the end of the line: the action history shows no markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor action for the rest of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, borrowers with high-rate federal loans kept paying their original interest rates and origination fees, and the Treasury kept collecting the spread between what it charges borrowers and what it pays to borrow. FFEL lenders and loan servicers kept their existing business untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury, FFEL lenders, and servicers

sides.party_line_note: 26 of the bill's 28 cosponsors were Democrats; the two Republicans put it over into nominal bipartisan territory, but the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill pays off outstanding FFEL loans and converts them to lower-rate Direct Loans, ending the ongoing interest stream and guarantee business built on loans issued before 2010. Borrowers win through lower rates; lenders lose the book of business.

Refinancing at Treasury plus 1% and repealing origination fees eliminates the interest spread and fees the loan program currently produces, revenue used for other education spending and deficit reduction. Taxpayers bear this cost, but the same spread is paid by borrowers out of pocket.
Moving FFEL loans into the Direct Loan program shifts servicing volume, though the loans still must be serviced. Servicing contracts would be reshuffled rather than eliminated.
